summary:
**BOOK 1: The Layton Court Mystery (Anthony Berkeley, 1926; Doubleday ed. 1929)**

**Preface:** Dedicated "To my Father." Author argues detective should be human, not a sphinx, and that all evidence should be given to the reader as found.

**Ch I, Eight o'Clock in the Morning:** Layton Court gardener William, melancholy, fights greenfly on a *Caroline Testout* rose. Roger Sheringham (author, 30s, Winchester and Oxford, stocky, round face, gray eyes, big-bowled pipe, baggy gray flannels, old Norfolk jacket) teases him. Roger meets Alexander "Alec" Grierson (big, cheerful, Oxford cricketer, engaged since the day before). Alec was coming from the lodge; claims he posted a letter to his bookmaker. Barbara Shannon (19, small, gray eyes, fair hair, firm chin) tells Alec she cannot marry him: "something very dreadful has happened."

**Ch II, An Interrupted Breakfast:** Host Victor Stanworth (~60, City financier, bachelor, St James's Street flat, Jacobean Layton Court in Hertfordshire rented for the summer). Late younger brother married Lady Cynthia Anglemere (eldest daughter of Earl of Grassingham); Stanworth settled £1,000/yr on her. Lady Stanworth is hostess. Guests: Mrs. Shannon (Barbara's mother, doll-like, complains about sleep), Major Jefferson (tall, sallow, taciturn ex-army secretary/dogsbody), Mary Plant (dark-haired, 26, husband in Soudanese Civil Service), Graves the butler (ex-prizefighter, huge). Jefferson called out by Graves. Lady Stanworth summons Roger and Alec: library door and windows locked inside; Stanworth not seen; bed unslept. Jefferson, Graves and Alec break the door (third try). Jefferson: "Mr. Stanworth appears to have shot himself."

**Ch III, Mr. Sheringham is Puzzled:** Library layout: French windows (lawn side), sash window over rose garden with window seat, small lattice window at left corner, door diagonal to it, fireplace facing French windows, typewriter table by door, black settee between sash window and fireplace, large writing table centre. Stanworth's body in chair behind table; revolver in right hand; small blackened hole at forehead centre. Typed note: "To Whom it May Concern. For reasons that concern only myself, I have decided to kill myself." Signature with earlier attempt "V-i-c." Lady Stanworth phones Dr. Matthewson and police (Elchester). Jefferson found searching the body's pockets. Roger walks Jefferson in garden; Jefferson keeps checking his watch. Roger finds Mrs. Plant at the safe, twisting its knob; she says she had given Stanworth her jewels to lock up; begs Roger not to give her away.

**Ch IV, Major Jefferson is Reluctant:** Inspector Mansfield (Elchester) is methodical. Notes typewriter use. Dr. Matthewson: dead ~8 hours, died ~2 a.m.; bullet under scalp; only one chamber fired; powder on wound. Matthewson had examined Stanworth for hay fever a few weeks earlier. Roger notes ashes in grate. Jefferson seems alarmed when safe opening is proposed; says he does not know the combination; keys found in upper waistcoat pocket, not usual lower one. Jefferson checks ink-pot for poison.

**Ch V, Mr. Sheringham Asks a Question:** Jefferson last saw Stanworth ~10 p.m. in garden with Roger (village church clock striking). Stanworth said no car needed in morning. Roger and Stanworth went in ~20 min later; Stanworth spoke to Mrs. Plant in hall, gave her roses. Alec saw Stanworth in garden. Inspector: no financial motive apparent; Stanworth had large Government stock. Roger and Alec suspect Jefferson; Roger asks why the wound is in centre of forehead, not above right eyebrow.

**Ch VI, Four People Behave Remarkably:** Roger's four suspicious people: Graves, Jefferson, Lady Stanworth (hated Stanworth), Mrs. Plant. Roger heard footsteps in corridor ~midnight–1 a.m. Keys probably put in wrong pocket by someone else. Broad scratch on Stanworth's right wrist. Alec privately thinks of Barbara's conduct but says nothing. Alec agrees to help on condition Roger takes no important step without telling him. Roger is "Sherlock," Alec "Watson."

**Ch VII, The Vase That Wasn't:** Roger notices the chimney-piece has only one blue vase; ring in the dust where the other stood; dust marks. Fragment of blue china on hearth rug. Barbara and Alec talk: "It hadn't anything to do with what's happened here"; she asks him to wait until they return from the Mertons' next month; they leave on the two forty-one train. Roger finds bullet mark in panel behind left pillar of chimney-piece; line from hole through the ring leads to the chair before the writing table.

**Ch VIII, Mr. Sheringham Becomes Startling:** Roger theorizes Stanworth fired at an intruder, then was murdered by the intruder pressing the revolver to his forehead. Alec objects: door and windows locked; confession. Roger proposes robbery motive (safe). Alec: "making a whole range of [mountains] out of a single worm-cast."

**Ch IX, Mr. Sheringham Sees Visions:** Graves sorts post: letters for Jefferson, Barbara, Mrs. Plant. Roger's imagined reconstruction. In the waste-paper basket Roger finds a sheet with "Victor St—" and blotted ink; blotter has fountain-pen scratches. Roger concludes the confession is a fake: Stanworth signed a sheet, pen flooded, murderer typed the statement above the signature. Roger: "that confession is a fake." Roger: "To find the murderer."

**Ch X, Mrs. Plant is Apprehensive:** Roger's theory: murderer premeditated, calculating. Alec objects: bullet fitted Stanworth's own shell. Roger suspects Mrs. Plant and Jefferson in league (Mrs. Plant's sudden cheerfulness at lunch). Roger tells Mrs. Plant she must testify at the inquest; she is alarmed and begs silence.

**Ch XI, Lady Stanworth Exchanges Glances:** Inspector opens safe with combination from makers. Papers: share certificates, contracts. Cash-box: over £4,000 in banknotes. Mrs. Plant's green leather jewel-case: necklace, bracelets, rings (modest value). Lady Stanworth identifies them as Mrs. Plant's. Lady Stanworth snubs inspector; Jefferson insists nothing important will be found. Roger notes Lady Stanworth's odd glances and apprehension.

**Ch XII, Hidden Chambers and What-Nots:** Roger and Alec search for a secret door: panels sound hollow; fireplace bricked up; walls ~18 inches. Jefferson enters briefly, says Lady Stanworth and Mrs. Plant are in their rooms, and he must go to Elchester. Roger tests door (lock intact), French windows (bolts), lattice window, sash window (anti-burglar fitting). Roger: "wizard in a small way." Alec: maybe suicide after all.

**Ch XIII, Mr. Sheringham Investigates a Footprint:** Roger demonstrates: lattice window handle balanced so it drops into its socket when pushed shut, letting murderer leave and lock it from outside. Footprint in flower bed below window, toe toward window: heel deeper, so man stepped backward from sill; large boot (~10 or 11). A second print nearly a yard and a half away on the path. Roger wants all male boots fitted. Someone leaves library by door as they watch. Jefferson's car (blue Sunbeam, chauffeur Chapman) waits at front to take Jefferson to Elchester; he left about four minutes after Roger and Alec. Roger wonders if Jefferson overheard them.

**Ch XIV, Dirty Work at the Ash Pit:** Ash pit behind outhouses. Roger finds grimy pencil note in Stanworth's hand: "...frightened almost out of my... this neighbourhood... serious danger... that brute Prince... fright of my life this morning on chancing to... be locked up." Roger concludes murderer is "Prince." Lodge: Mrs. William (William's wife, round-faced, twinkling eyes) says gates shut ~10 p.m.; Halbert the showman; Prince (John Prince) is "dangerous," attacked Stanworth once, works at Hillcrest Farm for Mr. Wetherby (~1.5 miles). Stanworth had been friendly with Wetherby.

**Ch XV, Mr. Sheringham Amuses an Ancient Rustic:** Village pub landlord (Albert): Prince was at Helchester Agricultural Show, won a prize; Wetherby back ~7 p.m.; Prince came back late. Prince is ~6 feet, stooped, strong, clever, "cunning." At Hillcrest Farm an old rustic directs them to Prince in next field. A bull chases them; Alec outruns Roger; Roger falls in ditch. Rustic laughs: "You want ter be very careful o' that there Prince John."

**Ch XVI, Mr. Sheringham Lectures on Neo-Platonism:** Station only half-dozen trains daily, none after 7 p.m.; no stranger seen. Roger lectures Alec on neo-Platonism. William (in greenhouse, vine and steps) says a very large stranger came up drive ~8:30 p.m. the night before, said by the lodge-wife to be the cook's brother (cook later seen on his arm). Roger finds the footprints in the flower bed smoothed out; concludes Jefferson heard them.

**Ch XVII, Mr. Grierson Becomes Heated:** Tea. Inquest tomorrow 11 a.m., in morning room. Mrs. Plant nervous; Roger baits her about Stanworth; she sharply refuses. Alec angry at Roger bullying women. Roger finds a blue vase fragment and more pieces in the laurel shrubbery between library and dining room. Roger reasons the murderer threw them there, so he returned to the house.

**Ch XVIII, What the Settee Had to Tell:** Roger and Alec: murderer probably lived in house or contacted someone inside. Roger finds a woman's handkerchief between settee cushions; scent recognized as jasmine. Face powder on settee arm; long fair hair. Alec reveals his engagement to Barbara is broken off. Roger seals hair in envelope.

**Ch XIX, Mr. Sheringham Loses and Wins the Same Bet:** Roger questions maids Alice and Mary: library tidied after dinner; settee cushions shaken, no pen there. At dinner Roger bets on who visited which rooms: Lady Stanworth (drawing room, morning room with Jefferson, upstairs); Mrs. Plant (drawing room only). Scent: "Amour des Fleurs" (guinea) vs. "Parfum Jasmine" (9s 6d). Jefferson, asked about Stanworth's finances, says he had five bank accounts; reveals butler's real name is Bill Higgins. Roger confronts Mrs. Plant with the handkerchief; she blanches. Alec wants to quit; Roger insists on going on.

**Ch XX, Mrs. Plant Proves Disappointing:** Mrs. Plant claims she gave jewels to Stanworth in the library, fearing she'd have to testify. Roger suspects she lies about the time. Roger tells her to correct her statement to the inspector. Roger proposes searching Stanworth's papers at night in the morning room (Jefferson working there); Alec agrees reluctantly.

**Ch XXI, Mr. Sheringham is Dramatic:** Roger visits Jefferson in morning room; helps tabulate Stanworth's holdings; Roger decides Jefferson is shy and honest. Later at night, Roger and Alec examine passbooks: five accounts; two in Stanworth's name, three in other names; large cash deposits (£1,000, £5,000). Roger: "Old Stanworth was a professional blackmailer!"

**Ch XXII, Mr. Sheringham Solves the Mystery:** Morning in rose garden. Roger's theory: Jefferson, in love with Mrs. Plant, killed Stanworth when he found him blackmailing her. Alec rejects it. Roger insists on pursuing the truth.

**Ch XXIII, Mrs. Plant Talks:** Inquest (morning room): verdict "Suicide during temporary insanity." Roger tells Mrs. Plant he knows she was blackmailed. She confesses: something before her marriage, unknown to husband; Stanworth demanded £250 within three months; she gave jewels; Stanworth had said he would tell husband. She swears Jefferson never came into the library that night. Stanworth kept evidence in a sealed envelope addressed to her husband. Afterwards she received a typed letter from Stanworth, posted from village by 8:30 post, saying he had burned the evidence and would kill himself.

**Ch XXIV, Mr. Sheringham is Disconcerted:** Roger realizes a posted letter means Stanworth could not have posted it after death... Alec says he always doubted murder. Roger checks with Mrs. Plant: letter typewritten, postmarked village, 8:30 post. Roger confronts Jefferson: "Where were you at the time Stanworth died?" Jefferson refuses, then speaks of Roger's suspected blackmail. Lady Stanworth enters.

**Ch XXV, The Mystery Finally Refuses to Accept Mr. Sheringham's Solution:** Jefferson's story: in India, a pal forged a check; Jefferson confessed to take blame; Stanworth got the check, forced Jefferson into his job. Lady Stanworth and Jefferson were secretly married ~six months earlier. Jefferson was with his wife the night of the death. Lady Stanworth had been forced by Stanworth into marrying his brother Victor, under threat of exposing her father, the earl. Roger apologizes; accepts Jefferson's alibi.

**Ch XXVI, Mr. Grierson Tries His Hand:** Jefferson describes Stanworth's blackmail; Graves was Stanworth's victim too (could have been hanged). Stanworth's letter came before lunch; Jefferson says it was "almost too good to be true." Alec proposes an unknown blackmail victim as murderer. Roger still doubts.

**Ch XXVII, Mr. Sheringham Hits the Mark:** Train to Victoria. Roger declares he has solved it: Alec killed Stanworth. Roger shows his reasoning: the hair belonged to Barbara; footprints matched Alec's; lattice window trick; Alec's presence; Alec's ignorance of the footprint. Roger asks why Alec killed Stanworth.

**Ch XXVIII, What Really Did Happen:** Alec's account: that night he went to library in pyjamas, hid behind curtains. Mrs. Plant was there crying; Stanworth blackmailed her. Barbara then came; Stanworth blackmailed her about her mother (Mrs. Shannon), demanding Barbara marry Alec within a month and pay money. Barbara defied him and left. Alec confronted Stanworth; Stanworth fired and missed (hit vase); Alec twisted revolver to Stanworth's forehead and fired. Alec burned ~16–17 envelopes of evidence in grate; typed letters to Mrs. Plant, Jefferson and Barbara; typed confession; hid the broken vase fragments in shrubbery. Left through lattice window, re-entered via dining room. Roger advises Alec never to tell Barbara. Alec considers going to police; Roger: "for heaven's sake, do try sometimes not to be so disgustingly conventional!"
*The End.*

*Transcriber's notes: first published 1926 anonymously as "?"; Doubleday, Doran & Co. 1929 text used; corrections to typos.*

**BOOK 2: Thomas Wingfold, Curate, Vol. I (George MacDonald; Gutenberg #5973)**

**Ch I, Helen Lingard:** Gray November wind. Helen (23, tall, blue-eyes, dark hair, fair skin, "over-still" face) sits in aunt's house at Glaston reading a novel whose heroine marries an unworthy man. She feels bored; sleeps through the afternoon. Her father, an Indian army officer, married a Hindoo lady; father died leaving fortune to Helen and brother Leopold (called Poldie, three years younger). Helen's mother died at her birth.

**Ch II, Thomas Wingfold:** Curate Thomas Wingfold (26) walks by the river below Osterfield Park, recites Horace, reflects that he entered the church as a profession; doubts nothing, believes nothing firmly. He has a dead brother. He takes his stipend from an absentee rector.

**Ch III, The Diners:** Mrs. Ramshorn (Helen's aunt, widow of Dean of Halystone, bitter, peevish) hopes her nephew George Bascombe (handsome, self-assured, Hercules-like barrister in training) will marry Helen. Wingfold is invited as foil. Bascombe is open-minded, skeptical, "good fellow." Wingfold seems insignificant, has hesitant "Don't you think?"

**Ch IV, Their Talk:** Dinner conversation on Horace, poetry, common sense; Bascombe's sneers at poets. Bascombe sings his own song "Each man has his lampful." Helen plays piano woodenly. Helen dislikes the song as "heathenish."

**Ch V, A Staggering Question:** On walk home, Bascombe asks Wingfold: "do you believe one word of all that?" Wingfold cannot answer; Bascombe says Wingfold is a humbug and that his silence shows honesty.

**Ch VI, The Curate in the Churchyard:** Wingfold sits on a gravestone. Reflects on Bascombe's taunts, his own inability to prove God; thinks of Paley and Butler. Recognizes his profession's weakness; resolves to study.

**Ch VII, The Cousins:** Bascombe's philosophy: a "prophet" of new order; denies religion; believes in duty to society; says he has no unknown region of thought. Helen's character: capable but unawakened. Mrs. Ramshorn's garden described.

**Ch VIII, The Garden:** Helen and Bascombe in garden. He smokes; she likes weaker tobacco. He preaches "mutual compassion" and argues against threats and promises. Helen half-persuaded; he begins to see her as a possible wife.

**Ch IX, The Park:** Walk through park; they go to the old deserted house in the hollow with lake; a childhood hiding place (trap in closet floor, sub-chamber); story of drowned lady's ghost. They meet the dwarfs.

**Ch X, The Dwarfs:** The dwarf woman (Rachel) and her uncle (Polwarth, asthmatic) pass. Bascombe calls them monsters, advocates eugenics and punishment. Helen mildly rebukes him. Church service; Wingfold preaches a dull sermon on forgiveness; Mrs. Ramshorn says forgetting injuries is not required. Helen loves brother Leopold: Eton, Cambridge; Hindoo mother's eyes.

**Ch XI, The Curate at Home:** Wingfold's spiritual crisis; hates his position; reads uncle's sermons (uncle Jonah Driftwood, D.D., left 157 sermons). Prayers fail; he doubts God's existence.

**Ch XII, An Incident:** Wingfold returns a dropped manuscript volume to Rachel and Polwarth on the road. Rachel smiles; Wingfold walks boldly after a child's smile. Birth agony of his soul.

**Ch XIII, A Report of Progress:** Bascombe courts Helen; she accepts his teachings. Wingfold's and Helen's paths separate.

**Ch XIV, Jeremy Taylor:** Letter signed Joseph Polwarth, The Park-Gate: the curate's sermon was Jeremy Taylor's. Wingfold ashamed; resolves to confess.

**Ch XV, The Park Gate:** Wingfold visits Park Gate lodge; Rachel answers the door; Polwarth absent.

**Ch XVI, The Attic:** Polwarth's attic with books; discusses preaching, honesty, and sermons from other men's pens.

**Ch XVII, Polwarth's Plan:** Polwarth advises Wingfold to read the New Testament; to confess to congregation; Wingfold asks whether Jesus existed; Polwarth says find Jesus himself.

**Ch XVIII, Joseph Polwarth:** Polwarth's story: Cornish ancestry; father tall; brothers died young; brother Robert died; sister Rachel with £20/yr. Polwarth was bullied at school; had a secret den in attic; prayed; reading Matthew 1:21 ("he shall save his people from their sins") brought conversion. Polwarth: knowing Jesus, not proving God, is the way.

**Ch XIX, The Conclusion of the Whole Matter:** Wingfold agrees to read the New Testament and resolves to resign if no progress within a month. Polwarth promises sermon-material. Wingfold: "You are the first real friend I have ever had."

**Ch XX, A Strange Sermon:** Wingfold confesses from the pulpit, on text "Confessing your faults one to another," that he has preached others' sermons. Mrs. Ramshorn scandalized; Bascombe thinks Wingfold brave. Helen is present; Mrs. Ramshorn and Bascombe discuss sermon.

**Ch XXI, A Thunderbolt:** Night: Leopold appears at Helen's window, bloody, wild; confesses he has murdered a woman ("I am a murderer"); the police are after him. Helen takes him in, hides him. Blood on wristband.

**Ch XXII, Leopold:** Helen agrees to hide him. He reveals he has killed; she swears not to give him up. He is addicted to a drug.

**Ch XXIII, The Refuge:** Helen takes Leopold to the deserted house; hides him in the closet room. He fears the place; she sings him a childhood lullaby.

**Ch XXIV, Helen with a Secret:** Helen returns home; keeps her secret; fears George would give Leopold up.

**Ch XXV, A Daylight Visit:** Helen visits Leopold in the day; takes his bloodied shirt away; considers prayer. Rachel sings at the lodge.

**Ch XXVI, Leopold's Story:** Leopold (before college) courted Emmeline, eldest daughter of a manufacturer neighbour; she flirted and was engaged to Captain Hodges (a dragoon). Leopold became addicted to a drug.

**Ch XXVII, Leopold's Story Concluded:** At a ball Leopold wore a mask and cloak; Emmeline took a note "Meet me for one long minute at the circle." In a wooded hollow she said she was marrying Captain Hodges and kissed him; Leopold stabbed her with a skean-dhu (Highland knife), fled, and went to Helen.

**Ch XXVIII, Sisterhood:** Helen learns the story. Helen takes Leopold's knife (his name engraved on silver handle). She feels a devotion to protect him.

**Ch XXIX, The Sick-Chamber:** Leopold shrieks; Helen brings him to her own room; aunt Mrs. Ramshorn agrees to help. Doctor Mr. Faber (new Glaston doctor; skeptical, cold) treats Leopold's brain fever. Leopold slowly recovers. Helen gradually gains a sense of her life's worth.

**Ch XXX, The Curate's Progress:** Polwarth tutors Wingfold in the New Testament. Discussion: Christ's primary mission; miracles. Polwarth prays for Wingfold.

**Ch XXXI, The Curate Makes a Discovery:** Wingfold reads "Why call ye me Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?" and "If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine." Wingfold resolves to obey Jesus; visits "a certain grievous old woman."

**Ch XXXII, Hopes:** Helen goes to church. Leopold, weak, asks why she attends; wants to see Bascombe. Helen believes Leopold may be innocent (perhaps delusion from drug).

**Ch XXXIII, The Ride:** Helen rides with Bascombe. Bascombe argues against immortality; then tells Helen about the murder of the young lady in the wood: a coast-guardsman saw a man jump into a boat; no trace. Bascombe says he would like to investigate; says a murderer should be imprisoned. Helen turns homewards.

*END OF THE FIRST VOLUME.*
